newsitem.title: USA: Mass gets something old, something new in Cellucci.
newsitem.headline: Mass gets something old, something new in Cellucci.

text.p: After seven years in the long shadow of William Weld, Paul Cellucci will be stepping into the limelight when he becomes acting governor of Massachusetts on Tuesday.

As a man who has spent his entire adult life in public office, first as a selectman for his small town, then as a state representative and state senator, it was Cellucci who helped Weld gain credit for cutting taxes 12 times in the last seven years and bringing the state's chaotic finances under control.

Where the glib, red-headed, six-foot-two Weld is a Harvard millionaire who can trace his blue-blood back to the 17th century, Cellucci grew up in the small town of Hudson, some 30 miles west of Boston cleaning cars at his family's Oldsmobile dealership.
The five-foot-eight Cellucci, whose black hair is now streaked with gray, graduated from Boston College Law School.

Unlike Weld, Cellucci has faced some financial crisis during his 20 years in public service. The Boston Globe revealed last December that he owed creditors more than $750,000, including nearly $70,000 in credit cards. As acting governor, Cellucci will get an immediate $15,000 a year raise bringing his salary to $90,000 annually.

The 49-year-old father of two "reflects the average citizen in Massachusetts," said House Speaker Thomas Finneran. The Democratic leader said of Cellucci's debt, "I think almost any mother or father with a child in college can empathize with Paul Cellucci."
Weld and Cellucci are very similar ideologically, observers note.

"But people forget that Paul Cellucci was one of the first fiscal conservative-social moderates in the state house," said Raymond Howell, a close adviser to both men. He noted that "Paul has been pro-choice, pro-gay rights and pro-diversity long before all those things were fashionable in Republican politics."
Other political observers are looking forward to Cellucci taking formal hold of the reins as acting governor for the remaining 18 months of Weld's term.

"It means this state will have a full-time governor for a change," Joan Manard, state Democratic Party chairwoman said. "I wish Bill Weld well, but he seems to be very interested in things, but for a very short period of time. Paul Cellucci is someone who is very involved and very committed to being governor."

Cellucci will have the advantage of being acting governor for a full year before he will have to seek re-election. Massachusetts Treasurer and fellow Republican Joseph Malone announced last week his intention of running for governor.
